what_its_for: Sodium fluoride helps prevent cavities and tooth decay by making your teeth stronger and more resistant to acid attacks from bacteria in your mouth. It is also used to treat sensitive teeth and may be prescribed if your drinking water does not have enough fluoride, especially in children during tooth development.
how_to_take: Sodium fluoride comes in several forms: tablets, drops, rinse (mouthwash), gel, or toothpaste. For tablets or drops: swallow them or let them dissolve in your mouth as directed by your dentist or doctor. For rinse: swish the liquid around in your mouth for about 1 minute, then spit it out — do not swallow. For gel or prescription toothpaste: brush your teeth thoroughly, then spit out — do not swallow. Always follow the specific instructions on your label, as directions may differ depending on the form you are using.
dosing: The dose depends on your age, the form of fluoride you are using, and how much fluoride is already in your drinking water. Children under 3: usually 0.25 mg per day if prescribed. Children 3–6 years: typically 0.5 mg per day. Children 6 and older and adults: usually 1 mg per day for supplements, or use rinse/gel as directed (often once daily at bedtime). Always follow your dentist or doctor's exact instructions and never use more than prescribed.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose, take or use it as soon as you remember. However, if it is almost time for your next dose, skip the missed dose and continue with your regular schedule. Do not double up to make up for a missed dose.
storage: Store sodium fluoride at room temperature, between 59°F and 77°F (15°C–25°C). Keep it away from heat, moisture, and direct sunlight. Keep all fluoride products tightly closed and out of reach of children, as too much fluoride can be harmful if swallowed in large amounts. Do not freeze liquid forms.
what_to_avoid: Do not eat, drink, or rinse your mouth for at least 30 minutes after using fluoride rinse, gel, or toothpaste to allow the fluoride to work properly. Avoid swallowing fluoride rinse, gel, or toothpaste. Do not give fluoride supplements to children if your local water supply already has adequate fluoride levels — ask your dentist or doctor first. Avoid taking fluoride supplements with dairy products (like milk or calcium) at the same time, as calcium can reduce how well fluoride is absorbed.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor or dentist if you or your child develops white, brown, or black spots on the teeth (this may be a sign of too much fluoride, called fluorosis). Seek emergency help immediately if a child swallows a large amount of fluoride — contact Poison Control at 1-800-222-1222. Also call your doctor if you experience nausea, vomiting, stomach pain, unusual weakness, or increased drooling after taking fluoride.
when_it_works: Fluoride works continuously to strengthen your tooth enamel each time you use it. You may not notice a dramatic change right away, but with regular use over weeks to months, it helps protect your teeth from cavities and decay. Your dentist can monitor improvements during routine checkups.
special_populations: Children: Fluoride supplements are generally recommended only when the local water supply has low fluoride content. Do not use adult-strength products in young children. Children under 6 should only use a tiny, pea-sized amount of fluoride toothpaste and should be supervised to avoid swallowing. Pregnant or breastfeeding women: Talk to your doctor before using fluoride supplements. Small amounts of fluoride pass into breast milk, but it is generally considered safe at normal doses. Elderly patients: No special dose adjustments are typically needed, but good dental hygiene habits are especially important. Kidney disease: Use with caution, as fluoride is removed by the kidneys. Talk to your doctor if you have kidney problems.
